questionText: What is the difference between var, explicit types, and target-typed new in C#?
shortAnswer: var infers the type from the right-hand side at compile time, explicit types state it directly, and target-typed new (new()) infers the type from the left-hand side. All three are statically typed — none of them is dynamic.
detailedAnswer: C# is statically typed: every variable has a compile-time type. var simply asks the compiler to infer it — int x = 5 and var x = 5 produce identical IL. Explicit types (int x = 5) document intent and are required where inference is impossible (e.g. var x = null does not compile). Target-typed new, added in C# 9, removes the repeated type name in construction: List<string> names = new(); Dictionary<int, string> map = new() { [1] = "one" };. The type still exists at compile time; the compiler simply copies it from the target. Use var when the type is obvious from the right side (new, casts, method names that state the type), and explicit types when the right side is ambiguous (e.g. var result = GetData() hides the return type from the reader).
codeExample:
var count = 5;             // int, inferred
int total = 5;             // int, explicit
List<string> names = new(); // List<string>, target-typed new
// var greeting = null;    // does NOT compile: no type to infer
internalWorking: Type inference happens entirely in the compiler frontend. The inferred type is baked into the assembly metadata exactly as if you had written it. There is zero runtime cost and no reflection involved.
realWorldUsage: In ASP.NET Core codebases, var dominates for new-expressions and well-named factory calls, while DTO and entity declarations stay explicit so API contracts read clearly in code review.
commonMistake: Believing var is dynamic. var x = 5; x = "hello"; fails to compile, whereas dynamic x = 5; x = "hello"; compiles and resolves at runtime.
technicalConversation: A reviewer may ask why you chose var over an explicit type in a given line — the answer should reference readability of that specific line, not a blanket rule.
interviewFollowUp: When does var fail to compile, and what does that tell you about what the compiler needs?
keyTakeaway: All three forms are statically typed. Pick the form that makes the type clearest to the human reader of that line.

questionText: What is the difference between value types and reference types in C#?
shortAnswer: Value types (struct, int, bool) hold their data directly and are copied on assignment; reference types (class, string, arrays) hold a pointer to data on the heap, so assignment copies the pointer and both variables observe the same object.
detailedAnswer: Value types store their data inline — in a local variable slot, or inside the containing object. Assigning one value type to another copies every field, so later mutations are independent. Reference types store a reference (pointer) to an object on the managed heap; assignment copies only the reference, so two variables can alias the same object and mutations through one are visible through the other. Method arguments follow the same rule: value-type parameters receive a copy (unless passed with ref/in/out), reference-type parameters receive a copy of the reference — the method can mutate the object's state but cannot make the caller's variable point elsewhere (unless ref is used). Structs should be small (rule of thumb: under 16 bytes) and immutable; larger or mutable shapes belong in classes. Nullable value types (int?) are the Nullable<T> struct, while nullable reference types (string?) are a compile-time annotation tracked by the compiler's null-state analysis.
internalWorking: Value types live where they are declared: locals on the stack (or enregistered), fields inline in their object. Reference-type objects live on the GC heap with an object header (sync block + method table pointer); locals hold a managed pointer to them. Copying a struct emits a field-by-field copy (cpblk for large structs); copying a reference is a single pointer copy.
realWorldUsage: DTOs and entities are classes (identity + shared mutation are desired). Small immutable values — dates, money, coordinates — are structs or readonly record structs so copying is cheap and aliasing bugs are impossible.
commonMistake: Mutating a struct returned from a property or collection (e.g. order.LineItems[0].Quantity = 5 when LineItem is a struct) — you mutate a temporary copy and the change is silently lost. Make such types immutable or classes.
technicalConversation: If a candidate says structs are always faster, ask about a 64-byte struct passed by value through three method calls versus a class — copying cost versus GC pressure is the real trade-off.
interviewFollowUp: Why is string, a reference type, often described as behaving like a value type?
keyTakeaway: Assignment copies data for value types and pointers for reference types. Choose struct for small immutable values, class for identity and shared state.

questionText: What is boxing and unboxing, and why should you avoid it in hot paths?
shortAnswer: Boxing wraps a value type in a heap object (e.g. passing int to a method taking object); unboxing extracts it back with a type check. Each box allocates memory and each unbox costs a check — in loops this creates GC pressure.
detailedAnswer: Boxing occurs whenever a value type is converted to object, dynamic, or a non-generic interface it implements (e.g. int passed as IEnumerable, string.Format("{0}", number), or adding an int to an ArrayList). The runtime allocates a new heap object, copies the value into it, and returns the reference. Unboxing ((int)obj) checks the object's type matches and copies the value back out to the stack. The costs are: one heap allocation per box (GC pressure), a type check per unbox, and potential InvalidCastException if the type mismatches. In hot paths — tight loops, high-throughput APIs — repeated boxing shows up as Gen0 allocations in profilers. The fixes are generics (List<int> instead of ArrayList — no boxing at all), overloads that take concrete value types, and being careful with non-generic APIs (Hashtable, string.Format with value types, IComparable without generics). Modern .NET also boxes less: interpolated string handlers and generic math reduce common cases.
internalWorking: The box instruction allocates an object of the value type's method table, memcpys the stack value into it. Unbox.any checks the method table pointer then copies the payload. The JIT cannot eliminate these because the heap object's identity is observable (ReferenceEquals, locking).
realWorldUsage: Legacy non-generic collections and reflection-heavy code (MethodInfo.Invoke boxes return values and arguments) are the usual production sources. Replacing ArrayList/Hashtable with generic collections is a standard modernization win.
commonMistake: Calling GetType() or using lock on a value type — both box first, so lock(valueType) locks a fresh object every time and provides zero mutual exclusion.
technicalConversation: If a profile shows Gen0 spikes in a parsing loop, boxing in string formatting or non-generic calls is one of the first suspects — ask how they would confirm (allocation profiler, e.g. dotTrace or PerfView).
interviewFollowUp: Why can't the JIT simply optimize boxing away?
keyTakeaway: Boxing = heap allocation + copy + later GC. Prefer generics and typed overloads; treat boxing in hot paths as a defect.

questionText: Why are strings immutable in .NET, and how should you build strings efficiently?
shortAnswer: Strings are immutable so they are thread-safe, hash-stable for dictionary keys, and shareable via interning. Because every concatenation allocates a new string, loops must use StringBuilder (or string.Create / interpolated handlers) instead of +=.
detailedAnswer: Immutability means once created, a string's characters never change — Substring, Replace, ToUpper all return new strings. This gives three guarantees: thread safety without locks, stable hash codes (a Dictionary<string, T> key cannot mutate under you), and safe interning (the runtime can reuse one "error" literal everywhere). The price is allocation: s += part in a loop of N iterations creates N intermediate strings and copies O(N^2) characters. The standard fix is StringBuilder, which maintains a mutable char buffer and produces one string at the end via ToString(). For small fixed counts (2–4 parts), plain interpolation or Concat is fine and often faster than StringBuilder (the threshold is a rule of thumb, confirmed by BenchmarkDotNet when it matters). DefaultInterpolatedStringHandler in modern .NET already reduces allocations for $"..." expressions. Also relevant: string.Create with Span for zero-waste building, and string.Intern only when you have many duplicates with long lifetimes (it pins entries in a way that can backfire).
internalWorking: A string is a sequential object: length prefix + UTF-16 chars inline. Concat allocates the exact final length and block-copies. StringBuilder holds a linked list of char[] chunks (doubling strategy) and ToString() allocates once and copies each chunk. Interned literals live in the intern pool and are never collected (until .NET 7+ collectible assemblies scenarios).
realWorldUsage: CSV/report generation, SQL building (prefer parameters — concatenation is also an injection risk), log message construction in tight loops, and HTML rendering in minimal APIs.
commonMistake: Using == on strings and assuming reference comparison — == is overloaded for value comparison (ordinal by default? No! == on string is ordinal value comparison; but Equals with StringComparison should be explicit for culture-sensitive code). Related mistake: ToLower() for case-insensitive comparison instead of string.Equals(a, b, StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase), which also avoids allocations.
technicalConversation: Ask what Ordinal vs CurrentCulture comparison means for a Turkish user searching "file" — the dotted-I problem makes culture-aware comparison a correctness issue, not a performance one.
interviewFollowUp: When would you choose string.Create over StringBuilder?
keyTakeaway: Immutable strings give safety; StringBuilder (or interpolation for small cases) gives speed. Never += in a loop.

questionText: What is the difference between a field, a property, and an auto-property, and when would you use each?
shortAnswer: A field is raw storage; a property is a get/set method pair that encapsulates storage; an auto-property is compiler-generated storage plus accessors. Expose properties (never public fields) so validation, change notification, or lazy logic can be added without breaking callers.
detailedAnswer: Fields (private int _count) are implementation detail — memory slots with no interception. Properties (public int Count { get { return _count; } set { if (value < 0) throw ...; _count = value; } }) compile to get_Count/set_Count methods, so they can validate, raise events (INotifyPropertyChanged), compute on demand, or set breakpoints. Auto-properties (public int Count { get; set; }) make the compiler generate the backing field and trivial accessors — identical IL to hand-written trivial properties, so there is no performance cost. Guidelines: public surface = properties always (binary compatibility: changing field→property later breaks compiled callers); required init-time data → { get; init; }; computed values → getter-only properties (public decimal Total => Price * Quantity); validation → full property with backing field; lazy expensive values → Lazy<T> behind a getter. Records build on this: positional records are init-only auto-properties with value equality.
internalWorking: Properties are metadata (PropertyDef) pointing at accessor methods; the JIT inlines trivial accessors, so auto-properties perform exactly like fields. The backing field of an auto-property gets an unspeakable name (<Name>k__BackingField) and is serialized by serializers that include fields unless configured otherwise.
realWorldUsage: EF Core maps properties to columns (needs a setter — private is fine); System.Text.Json serializes public properties by default; WPF/MAUI binding requires properties (fields are invisible to the binding engine).
commonMistake: Public fields in DTOs/entities, or auto-properties with logic expectations — e.g. assuming { get; set; } validates. Also: mutable struct properties (point.X = 5 fails to compile because the property returns a copy — the same copy semantics as the struct mistake).
technicalConversation: Ask whether a property should ever throw — getters that throw or perform I/O surprise callers (debuggers evaluate properties!). Side-effect-free getters are a widely followed guideline.
interviewFollowUp: Why does changing a public field to a property break already-compiled consumers?
keyTakeaway: Fields store, properties control. Public API = properties; pick auto, init-only, computed, or full based on what the member must guarantee.

questionText: When should you choose a class, a struct, or a record in C#?
shortAnswer: Class for identity and shared mutable state; struct for small (≤16 bytes), immutable values where copying is cheap; record (class) for immutable data with value equality; readonly record struct for small immutable values with value equality.
detailedAnswer: Start with class — it is the default for a reason: reference semantics, inheritance, cheap to pass around (one pointer), natural for services, entities, and DTOs with identity. Choose struct when the type is a small, logically singular value (a point, a currency amount, a date range) that should copy by value and never be null; keep it readonly and tiny, because every pass-by-value copies the whole payload and mutable structs cause lost-update bugs. Choose record when you want concise immutable data carriers with structural equality: positional syntax (public record User(string Name, int Age)), with-expressions for non-destructive mutation, and value-based ==/GetHashCode so two instances with the same data compare equal — ideal for DTOs, messages, and cache keys. readonly record struct combines both for hot-path values (e.g. parsing tokens). Performance note: class instances cost a heap allocation + GC; structs cost copies — measure at 16+ bytes. Equality note: class == is reference equality unless overloaded; record == is value equality; struct == does not exist unless you define it (use Equals, which boxes unless IEquatable<T> is implemented — implement it).
internalWorking: Records synthesize <Clone>$ methods, equality members, GetHashCode combining, and Deconstruct/ToString. Struct equality defaults to ValueType.Equals (reflection-based, slow — hence IEquatable<T>). with-expressions call the protected copy constructor then set init-only members.
realWorldUsage: API contracts and MediatR messages as records (equality helps idempotency checks and tests); EF entities as classes (identity + proxies need references); high-frequency parsing values as readonly record structs.
commonMistake: Records with mutable state (var properties) used as dictionary keys — mutation changes the hash code and the entry is lost. Also: positional record with a collection property — equality compares the collection reference, not contents.
technicalConversation: Ask when value equality is actively harmful: entities with database identity should compare by Id (or reference), not by all fields — two different rows with identical data are not the same entity.
interviewFollowUp: How does with-expression initialization interact with required members and validation?
keyTakeaway: Class = identity, struct = tiny immutable value, record = data + value equality. Match the semantics to the domain concept, not the syntax fashion.

questionText: What are the best practices for exception handling in C#?
shortAnswer: Catch only what you can handle, preserve stack traces (bare throw), throw the most specific exception, validate with guard clauses instead of exceptions for expected cases, and log once at the boundary — never swallow, never return null silently, never use exceptions for flow control.
detailedAnswer: The core rules: (1) Catch specific types (DbUpdateException, TimeoutException), never bare catch {} — and never catch Exception just to return null. (2) Re-throw with throw; not throw ex; — the latter resets the stack trace and destroys the crime scene. (3) Prefer guard clauses (ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull) for predictable invalid input; exceptions are for exceptional conditions, and throwing costs ~microseconds plus a stack walk. (4) Add context when wrapping: catch (SqlException ex) { throw new OrderStoreException(orderId, ex); } — inner exceptions preserve the chain. (5) Use finally or using for cleanup, not catch-and-continue. (6) Log once, at the outermost boundary (our middleware logs with correlation), not at every layer — duplicate logs are noise. (7) Exception filters (catch (Exception ex) when (retryable)) avoid unwinding the stack for conditions you will not handle. (8) For libraries: document thrown exceptions in XML docs; consider Result<T> or Try-patterns for expected failures (int.TryParse, Dictionary.TryGetValue) so callers are not forced into try/catch for control flow. (9) Never throw from finally blocks, Dispose, or finalizers — it masks the original error.
internalWorking: Throwing builds an Exception object capturing the stack trace (StackTrace captures frames; in Release with optimizations, inlined frames may be missing). First-chance exceptions notify the debugger before any handler runs. Filters run before the stack unwinds, so the original call stack is intact if the filter declines.
realWorldUsage: ASP.NET Core: global middleware (like ours) handles logging + envelope mapping; controllers/services throw domain exceptions (NotFoundException etc.) instead of formatting HTTP responses. Background workers: catch per-message so one poison message does not kill the consumer.
commonMistake: catch (Exception) { /* ignore */ } — the silent killer that turns data corruption into a mystery. Second: throw ex; destroying traces. Third: throwing exceptions for validation of user input on hot paths instead of returning validation results.
technicalConversation: Ask how they distinguish 'log and continue' from 'fail fast' — the answer should reference blast radius: a failed background email can log-and-continue; a failed payment write must fail loudly.
interviewFollowUp: Why are exception filters preferable to catching and re-throwing when probing for retryable errors?
keyTakeaway: Throw specific, catch specific, preserve traces, log once at the boundary. Exceptions are for the exceptional.

questionText: How do ref, out, and in parameters work, and when should each be used?
shortAnswer: ref passes a variable by reference for read/write (must be initialized first); out passes by reference for output-only (method must assign before returning); in passes by reference as read-only (avoids copying large structs). Use sparingly — return values and tuples are clearer.
detailedAnswer: By default arguments pass by value (a copy of the value or reference). ref makes the parameter an alias to the caller's variable: reads and writes affect the caller, the variable must be definitely assigned before the call, and both sides mark ref. out is the output twin: the caller may pass an unassigned variable, but the method must assign it on every exit path — the classic TryParse pattern (bool TryGetValue(key, out TValue value)). in passes a readonly reference: no copy of large structs, compiler-enforced read-only (writing to an in parameter is a compile error; note that calling methods on it may defensively copy if the struct is not readonly). Modern guidance: prefer returning tuples/records over out (deconstruction reads better: var (ok, value) = TryGet(...)), reserve ref for high-performance struct mutation (Span<T>-based parsers), and use in only for provably large readonly structs after profiling — for small structs, by-value is as fast or faster (enregistration). All three require the keyword at both declaration and call site, which keeps the aliasing visible.
internalWorking: ref/out/in all compile to managed pointers (byref) passed to the method — no copying. The definite-assignment rules are compiler flow analysis. in parameters on non-readonly structs trigger defensive copies at each member access (the compiler cannot prove the method won't mutate), which can make in slower than by-value — hence readonly struct.
realWorldUsage: Try-patterns across the BCL; high-performance parsing (Utf8Parser takes Span and out); interop/PInvoke signatures where native code writes through pointers.
commonMistake: Overusing out for multiple returns instead of tuples — (bool ok, User user) is clearer. Also: capturing a ref local in a lambda or async method — not allowed (ref cannot escape the stack frame), which surprises people refactoring sync code to async.
technicalConversation: Ask why async methods cannot have ref/out parameters — the state machine may resume on another thread/stack after await, but a byref must always point at a live stack location.
interviewFollowUp: What is a ref struct (Span<T>) and why does it have the same escaping restrictions?
keyTakeaway: ref = in/out alias, out = guaranteed output, in = readonly alias. Default to return values; reach for byref only for Try-patterns and measured performance.

questionText: What are constructors, static constructors, and object initializers, and what ordering guarantees exist?
shortAnswer: Instance constructors initialize new objects (chained with this/base); static constructors initialize static state once per type before first use; object initializers set accessible properties after construction. Order: static fields/static ctor → instance fields → base ctor → this ctor → initializers.
detailedAnswer: Constructors: parameterless or parameterized; constructor chaining via this(...) reuses logic within the class, base(...) forwards to the parent — if omitted, the parameterless base constructor runs implicitly (compile error if none exists). Static constructors: parameterless, parameterless-access-modifier-less, run exactly once per AppDomain before the first instance is created or static member accessed; used for static data that needs logic (Regex, lookup tables). They must be fast and exception-free — a thrown exception poisons the type (TypeInitializationException on every later use). Object initializers (new User { Name = "x", Age = 3 }) run after the constructor and require accessible setters (set or init); collection initializers call Add. Required members (required keyword, C# 11) force callers to set values via constructor or initializer — enforced at compile time. Primary constructors (C# 12, class Point(int x, int y)) capture parameters as fields/parameters usable in initializers and member initializers. Records add copy constructors for with-expressions.
internalWorking: The compiler emits .ctor (instance) and .cctor (static, marked beforefieldinit unless explicit static ctor — beforefieldinit relaxes timing to 'before first static access'). Initializers are plain property sets emitted inline at the call site after newobj. Primary-constructor parameters become hidden fields/parameters captured by the class.
realWorldUsage: DI containers call the greediest public constructor (constructor injection); EF Core needs a parameterless constructor (can be private) plus property setters; serializers use parameterless ctor + initializers unless constructor binding is configured.
commonMistake: Calling virtual methods from constructors — the override runs on a half-constructed object (fields still default). Also: heavy I/O in static constructors causing first-request stalls and undebuggable TypeInitializationExceptions.
technicalConversation: Ask what happens when two threads race the first use of a type — the runtime takes a global lock around .cctor, so a blocking static constructor can deadlock the process (a classic production hang).
interviewFollowUp: How do required members change API design compared to constructor-only validation?
keyTakeaway: Constructors establish invariants, static ctors run once (keep them trivial), initializers are post-construction sugar. Never call virtuals from a ctor.

questionText: What is the difference between throw, throw ex, and ExceptionDispatchInfo, and why does it matter?
shortAnswer: throw re-throws preserving the original stack trace; throw ex; resets it to the current location; ExceptionDispatchInfo.Capture/Throw preserves traces across threads, tasks, and await boundaries.
detailedAnswer: When you catch an exception you sometimes must let it continue after logging or partial handling. bare throw; re-raises the same exception object with its original Watson buckets and stack intact — always preferred. throw ex; (or throw any named variable) starts a new stack trace at the throw site, deleting the original failure location — the single most common trace-destroying bug in enterprise code, and hard to spot in review because it looks intentional. ExceptionDispatchInfo covers the cases bare throw cannot: crossing thread/task boundaries. Example: an async method catches, stores ExceptionDispatchInfo.Capture(ex), and a different thread calls .Throw() later — the original stack (including the pre-await frames) is preserved, which a plain re-throw on another thread cannot do. The TPL uses this internally (AggregateException unwrapping, async state machines). Practical guidance: in catch blocks that only log/cleanup, use throw;; to transport errors across workers/queues, capture ExceptionDispatchInfo; in middleware-style boundaries, don't catch at all — let it bubble to the centralized handler.
internalWorking: Exceptions carry _stackTrace (frames) and _watsonBuckets (OS-level info). throw; leaves them untouched; throw ex; overwrites _stackTrace via Environment.GetStackTrace. ExceptionDispatchInfo stores the stack + buckets and restores them through the remote-stackTraceString mechanism on Throw(). Exception filters (when) execute during the first pass, before unwinding, so the stack is complete.
realWorldUsage: Message-queue consumers that defer poison-message rethrows, custom Polly-style retry helpers, test frameworks asserting throws, and any catch-log-continue boundary in workers.
commonMistake: catch (Exception ex) { logger.Error(ex); throw ex; } — the log looks fine but every downstream trace points at the middleware instead of the bug. Linters (CA2200: rethrow to preserve stack) flag exactly this.
technicalConversation: Ask the candidate to read a production trace that ends in their catch block — can they tell where it actually failed? If they used throw ex;, the answer is no, and that is the lesson.
interviewFollowUp: How do async/await state machines already use ExceptionDispatchInfo-like behavior, and where does it fall short?
keyTakeaway: throw; preserves, throw ex; destroys, ExceptionDispatchInfo transports. Default to bare throw and centralized handling.
